vignette:
The Weight She Carries Home

Amara is twenty-one years old, and she has already seen more than most people see in a lifetime. She grew up in a region of East Africa where conflict was not abstract - it was the sound of mortar fire two villages over, the smell of smoke on the wind. But nothing prepared her for what happened eighteen months ago, when the militia swept through the aid compound where she had been volunteering as a community health worker. She was the youngest person there by nearly a decade, and she was the one who had to pull a colleague's body behind a storage container while fighters moved through the courtyard. She stayed there for four hours, pressed against concrete, listening.

She made it out. Several others did not.

Within weeks of returning home, Amara enrolled in a counseling training program. People who know her describe this as remarkable resilience. Amara herself is not sure what to call it. She thinks, sometimes, that she chose the work because helping others is the only thing that quiets the noise in her head long enough for her to function. She sits across from clients every day - young people dealing with grief, displacement, family violence - and she listens carefully, asks the right questions, reflects their pain back to them with genuine warmth. She is good at her job. Her supervisor has told her so twice.

What her supervisor does not know is what happens after the sessions end.

Amara cannot sleep for more than two or three hours at a stretch. When she does sleep, she is back in that courtyard - not always the same scene, but always the same feeling: the absolute certainty that she is about to die. She wakes with her heart slamming against her ribs, drenched in sweat, and she sits on the edge of her bed in the dark and counts her breaths the way she teaches her clients to do, and sometimes it helps and sometimes it does not. In the mornings she is exhausted in a way that coffee does not touch.

During the day, the intrusions come without warning. A car backfiring on the street outside the counseling center sends her flat against the wall before she has consciously registered the sound. A client once described the smell of burning, and Amara had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she sat on the floor for eight minutes until the flashback loosened its grip. She told her supervisor she had a stomach bug that afternoon. She has become fluent in small, protective lies.

She does not talk about any of this to the people around her. Her mother worries enough. Her friends from home did not go to the compound, and she does not know how to explain what the compound did to her without also explaining what she saw there, and she is not ready to put words to that. She has started declining invitations - dinners, church, the small gatherings that used to feel easy. The world outside her apartment feels loud and unpredictable in a way it never did before, and she finds herself calculating exits whenever she enters a room, a habit she cannot seem to unlearn.

What troubles Amara most, though, is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance. It is the numbness that has settled over the parts of her life that used to bring her joy. She loved music once - she sang in a choir for six years. She has not sung since she came back. She picks up her phone to call her closest friend and puts it down again without dialing. She describes this flatness to herself as tiredness, because that is easier than naming what it might actually be.

She is twenty-one years old. She counsels other people through their trauma five days a week. And she has not told a single person that she is drowning.
